sentences.text: It has happened to her four times.
Eleven, thirteen, sixteen, and twenty-two.
Always at that pond, always with the dragonfly on that reed, always between three and six seconds, always the same summer on the other side.
She has been down to that pond, on a conservative estimate, four hundred times.
She has lain on that bank in July with a dragonfly on that reed perhaps sixty times.
Four.

That is the rate, and she puts it in whenever she tells this, because a story about a thing that happens is a completely different story from a story about a thing that has happened four times in eighteen years to one person with nobody else there.
She has never seen the boy again.
Three of the four times there was nobody on the far bank at all; once there was a bicycle lying on the grass by the jetty.
She has no mechanism and she is not going to offer one.

What she has is four occasions, two of which happened after she was old enough to be sceptical about the first two, and a photograph that she found afterwards and not before, which she thinks is the only part of the account that would interest anybody who does this properly.
She told her father in the November she was twenty-two, at the kitchen table, badly, over about twenty minutes.
He listened all the way through without interrupting, which is not like him.
Then he said: "Red T-shirt." "Yes." "I had that until I was about thirteen.
My mother hated it." He turned his cup round.
"What was I doing?" "Nothing.

Sitting on the jetty with your elbows on your knees looking at the reeds." And her father sat there for a while and then said the thing that Elin was not remotely prepared for, which was: "That'll be the summer my father was ill." He said that he had spent most of that July down at that pond because there was nothing to do at the house and because there were people in it all the time, and that he had sat on that jetty for hours, and that he could not now remember one single thing he had thought about in the whole of that month.
He said he had been fine.
He said he was not saying it had been bad.

He said that when he thought about that summer at all what he got was the pond and the heat and the smell of it and nothing else, and that he had never told anybody that and had not known he was going to tell her.
Her grandfather recovered, as it happens, and lived until 2011, and Elin knew him and he taught her to reverse a trailer.
That is the part that nearly everybody gets wrong when she tells it.
They want the summer to have been the last one.
It was not.

It was an ordinary frightening summer in the middle of a life that turned out fine, and the thing her father could not remember a single thought from was eleven weeks of being a boy at a pond while adults he loved were doing something difficult upstairs.
Elin is twenty-nine.

She goes down to the pond in July, most years, and lies on the bank on her front about three metres from the reeds, and waits for a dragonfly that is not the same dragonfly to land on the third reed from the left.
She has never once thought of anything she would say.
